blocks.text: Body cells carry thousands of genes on a limited number of chromosomes: humans have about 20,000 genes on 23 chromosomes (present in two sets), and the fruit fly Drosophila about 13,000 genes on 4 chromosomes (also in two sets). So many genes lie in a line on each chromosome, some very close together.

blocks.title: Linked genes
blocks.text: Genes present on the same chromosome are linked genes, and this is gene linkage. Closely linked genes tend to stay together and do not assort independently in gamete formation, while genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on one chromosome, assort independently.

Linkage and its frequency are studied by making crosses and counting how often each phenotype appears, comparing parental combinations (the same as the parents) with recombinant, or new, combinations.

items: Parental and new phenotypes in an equal 1:1:1:1 ratio: the genes are not linked and assort independently.
Parental combinations more frequent and new ones fewer: incomplete linkage; the genes are linked but can separate by crossing over.
Only parental combinations and no new ones: complete linkage; the genes are very close and do not separate.

blocks.text: The American biologist Thomas Hunt Morgan studied wing length and abdomen width in Drosophila: long wings (L) are dominant to short or vestigial wings (l), and a broad abdomen (B) is dominant to a narrow one (b). A broad-abdomen long-winged fly crossed with a narrow-abdomen vestigial-winged fly gave F1 flies with long wings and broad abdomens, and two F1 flies were then crossed.

blocks.alt: Left: an F1 fly's pair of homologous chromosomes, one carrying L and B, the other l and b. Top right: if the genes assorted independently F2 would be 9 long broad, 3 long narrow, 3 vestigial broad and 1 vestigial narrow, with the middle two marked new. Below: Morgan observed only 3 long broad and 1 vestigial narrow, both parental. Bottom: testcross results 1:1:1:1 mean not linked, many parental and few new mean incomplete linkage, only parental mean complete linkage.
blocks.caption: Gene linkage in Drosophila (original diagram after Figure 18.10).
blocks.long_description: Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. In the book's example the F1 fly carries long-wing L and broad-abdomen B on one chromosome and l and b on its homologue. Independent assortment would give a 9:3:3:1 F2 with two new combinations, but only the parental combinations appeared, in a 3:1 ratio, so the two genes do not assort independently. In general, a cross reveals linkage by comparing parental and new (recombinant) offspring: equal numbers mean the genes are not linked, fewer new types mean incomplete linkage broken by crossing over, and no new types mean complete linkage.

blocks.text: Independent assortment predicts a 9:3:3:1 F2 with two new combinations (long wings with narrow abdomen, vestigial wings with broad abdomen). Morgan observed only the parental combinations: 3/4 long wings with broad abdomen and 1/4 vestigial wings with narrow abdomen. He concluded that the genes for wing length and abdomen width lie on the same chromosome and do not assort independently.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: Gene linkage can only be observed when a cross produces a large number of offspring: the larger the progeny, the more likely it is to show the actual frequency of linkage in the population.
